title: Human-controlled AI release gate
summary: This intermediate checklist helps practitioners decide whether an AI-assisted change may proceed to release. It requires an authorized human decision based on documented criteria, evidence, monitoring, and a workable stop path.
prerequisites: The proposed change and its intended use
A person authorized to approve or reject the release

sections.title: Make the release decision
paragraphs: Should the release proceed? Release only when a named, authorized human has reviewed traceable evidence against written acceptance criteria, recorded an approval, and confirmed that monitoring and a workable stop path are in place. If any of those conditions is absent, hold the release and complete the missing control before reconsidering it.

Step 1: Confirm who has authority to approve or reject this release and record the scope of that authority. If no authorized person is available or the authority is unclear, pause the release and obtain an explicit assignment from the accountable owner.

Step 2: Assemble the decision evidence, including the intended use, evaluation results, known limitations, unresolved risks, monitoring plan, and stop procedure. If evidence is missing, inconsistent, or cannot be traced to the proposed change, block the release and obtain or repeat the relevant evaluation.

Step 3: Compare the evidence with acceptance criteria written before the decision. If criteria are absent or ambiguous, do not infer them from the results; have the accountable owner define and approve them, then repeat the comparison. If a criterion is not met, reject or hold the release, remediate the failure, and evaluate again.

Step 4: Have the authorized human record an approve, reject, or conditional decision with its rationale. A conditional decision permits release only after every stated condition has verifiable evidence. If a condition remains open, keep the release on hold and return it to the responsible person.

Step 5: Confirm that the release can be observed and stopped through the documented operating process. If monitoring does not expose the agreed warning signs or the stop procedure cannot be demonstrated, do not release; repair the missing control and test it again.

sections.title: Source correction and control rationale
paragraphs: The previous citation, content/resources/evaluation-safety/human-controlled-ai-release-gate.json, was an unregistered local path and had never been verified. The source record changed to the official National Institute of Standards and Technology publication listed at the end of this resource. This correction affects the provenance and verification of the checklist's risk-management rationale.

The cited framework organizes AI risk-management work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions. The gate applies those functions by requiring accountable human authority, a defined context and intended use, measured evidence, and an explicit decision about whether identified risk is acceptable or requires treatment.

Human approval is not a substitute for evidence. The approver uses documented evidence and criteria to make an accountable decision, records the rationale, and sends failed or incomplete cases back for remediation rather than allowing uncertainty to become an implicit approval.

sections.title: Expected evidence and verification
paragraphs: Expected evidence is a decision record that identifies the proposed release, the authorized human decision-maker, the acceptance criteria, the evidence reviewed, unresolved risks, the final decision, its rationale, and any release conditions. It also includes the monitoring plan and evidence that the stop procedure was tested.

Verify the gate by tracing every acceptance criterion to evaluation evidence and then tracing the recorded decision to the named authorized person. If a criterion lacks evidence or the decision lacks an accountable owner, the gate has not passed; hold the release and complete the missing record or evaluation.

Verify operational readiness by demonstrating that agreed warning signs can be observed and that the documented stop procedure reaches the responsible person and produces the intended halt. If the demonstration fails or cannot be reproduced, record the failure, repair the process, repeat the demonstration, and keep the release blocked until it succeeds.
